task_row_model.query: I have two independent groups (n = 15 each) and a continuous outcome that is not normally distributed. Which statistical test should I use to compare the groups, what assumptions should I check, and how should I report effect size and results?

documents.content: For two-sample comparisons of a continuous outcome, the Student's t-test or Welch's t-test are commonly used when data are approximately normally distributed. The pooled t-test assumes equal variances; Welch's t-test relaxes that assumption and is preferred if variances differ. If normality is violated, options include transforming the outcome (log, square-root) to approximate normality, or using bootstrap methods to estimate the sampling distribution of the mean difference. However, for small samples and clear non-normality, nonparametric approaches like the Mann–Whitney U may be more appropriate.

When outcomes vary with covariates, linear regression allows modeling the continuous response as a function of predictors, estimating adjusted differences between groups while controlling for confounders. Regression assumes linearity, independent errors, homoscedasticity, and normally distributed residuals for inference on coefficients. For non-normal outcomes or heteroskedasticity, robust standard errors or generalized linear models can be used. Reporting should include estimated coefficients, standard errors, confidence intervals, and model diagnostics. Regression is useful for adjusting for baseline imbalances, but it does not replace choosing the correct test for an unadjusted two-group comparison.

For two independent groups of n=15 measuring a continuous outcome that is not normally distributed, the recommended test is the Mann–Whitney U (Wilcoxon rank-sum) test. It compares the distribution of ranks between groups and is robust to departures from normality. Key assumptions: independent observations, ordinal or continuous outcome, and that the test primarily assesses differences in central tendency when distributions have similar shapes; if shapes differ, results reflect distributional differences. With n=15 per group, report exact or permutation p-values if software supports them. Also report effect size (rank-biserial or Cliff's delta), medians and IQRs, the U statistic and p-value, and interpret with confidence intervals when possible.

When comparing two independent samples with a continuous outcome that departs from normality, the Mann–Whitney U test (also called Wilcoxon rank-sum) is a nonparametric alternative to the t-test. It ranks combined observations and tests whether one group tends to have higher ranks than the other, making no assumption of normal distribution. The test does assume independent observations and similar shapes of distributions under the null; if distributions differ markedly in shape, interpretation as a location shift is problematic. For small samples, exact p-values or permutation tests can improve inference. Report medians and interquartile ranges alongside the test statistic and p-value.

Analysis of variance (ANOVA) compares means across three or more groups and decomposes total variance into between-group and within-group components. One-way ANOVA assumes independent observations, normally distributed residuals, and homogeneity of variances across groups; violations can be addressed with transformations or Welch's ANOVA. Significant ANOVA results warrant post-hoc pairwise comparisons with adjustments such as Tukey's HSD or Bonferroni correction. ANOVA is not typically used when there are only two groups, since it reduces to an equivalent t-test; it is mainly applicable when dealing with multiple factor levels or factorial designs.
